catalog_quote: [p.23] Dimasa is a tonal language with three register tones- high, mid and low. The sentence constructions end in falling intonation in the language with mostly trochaic word accents. This is a typical suprasegmental feature of the Bodo-Garo languages which share similar features with some of the Austro-Asiatic languages. [p.79] Dimasa has a simple tone system. It consists of a three-way contrast which is high, mid and low. These are register tones and are lexical in nature. ... These tones are limited to nouns, verbs, adjectives and some adverbs with free morphemes while the inflectional affixes do not carry tones except in cases of suffixation and tone sandhi. [p.88] It is often confusing to distinguish the suprasegmental features such as tone, intonation, stress, pitch and accent. All the dialects of Dimasa are tonal with some intonation only in polysyllables and sentences. Stress (primary) and accent (low and high) function only to distinguish different dialects in Dimasa. Tone in Dimasa is determined by vowel length and glottalisation in both low and high tone. [p.89] Longer words, which are polysyllabic, carry lexical intonation in each syllable while tone is marked at the final syllable in Dimasa.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dimasa is described as a register-tone language (H, M, L) in which stress/accent is not lexically contrastive ('functions only to distinguish dialects'); word accent is characterised in passing as 'mostly trochaic' (i.e. word-initial prominence in disyllables), while the single lexical tone of a word is realised on its final syllable. No fuller rule (syllable counting, weight) is given anywhere in the accessible literature.
new_statements.exceptions: 'mostly' trochaic (no exceptions listed); stress/accent said to vary between dialects (Hasao standard vs Hawar, Dembra, Dijuwa) without detail. Note the tension with other descriptions: Sarmah 2009 finds initial syllables of disyllables short (70 vs 120 ms) with lexical tone only on the final syllable, and Jacquesson 2008 / Evans & Langthasa 2024 describe weak, reducible first syllables (sesquisyllables) -- all pointing to final-syllable prominence rather than trochaic accent; none of them uses the word 'stress'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level typological remark (citation forms); the p.88 passage is in the intonation section and concerns dialect differentiation. Variety: Standard Hasao dialect (Haflong, Dima Hasao).
new_statements.identity_note: Longmailai 2014 describes the Standard Hasao dialect (Haflong, Dima Hasao district), the variety declared standard by the Dimasa Sahitya Sabha; Evans & Langthasa 2024 also Haflong; Rajioung 2021/2025 cover Hawar (Cachar), Dembra and Dijuwa dialects. All fall under glottocode dima1251 (no separate dialect glottocodes used). Longmailai states stress/accent differs between dialects.

Dimasa has register tones which are only lexical and Tedim Chin has register tones which are both lexical and grammatical in nature. … Dimasa has a simple tone system. It contrasts tone in three ways, high (‫)މ‬, mid (¯) and low (‫)ޘ‬ which are register tones. A minimal triplet for Dimasa tone is shown in (1). … In Dimasa, low tones can be long as kҦà ‘tie’ and it can be short and glottal nò࣯ ‘house’. sources.note: No stress statement. 'A sketch of phonology' pp.9-15: two tones (higher marked with superscript 2), weak/dropped vowels in first syllables (bV-, gV-, sV-, pV- prefixes). sources.note: The article is about sentence-level focus intonation, not the tone inventory: narrow focus raises the pitch range regardless of the lexical tone of the morpheme the focus marker attaches to, and focused sentences also carry tense phonation. It presupposes that Dimasa morphemes carry underlying lexical tone, which matches the catalog's tonal / lexical-tone entry without adding inventory detail.
